slides.0.title: Principal Red Grapes
slides.0.subtitle: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and GSM
slides.1.title: Syrah: the northern flagship
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The north's red grape
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Syrah underpins the reds of Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Joseph and Crozes-Hermitage; Cornas is 100% Syrah
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Parentage
slides.1.highlights.1.content: 1998 DNA research showed Syrah is a cross of Dureza (black) and Mondeuse Blanche (white), from the Rhône–Savoie area
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Flavour profile
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Black fruit, black pepper, olive and violet, with smoke, bacon and leather when ripe or aged
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Plantings
slides.1.highlights.3.content: About 22,200 ha across the Rhône in 2025, the second most planted variety (Inter Rhône)
slides.1.content: In the north Syrah shows cooler, peppery, floral character; in the south it is mostly a blending partner.
slides.2.title: Grenache: the southern heart
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Most planted red
slides.2.highlights.0.content: About 32,400 ha in 2025, far ahead of any other red (Inter Rhône)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Flavour and structure
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Red berries, spice and high alcohol, with comparatively pale colour and soft tannin, and a tendency to oxidise
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Old vines and bush training
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Often old bush-trained vines giving low yields and concentration
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Likely origin
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Often thought to come from Spain (the Aragón area); accounts vary
slides.2.content: Grenache supplies fruit and alcohol "flesh" and usually needs partners for colour and tannin.
slides.3.title: Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Carignan and others
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Mourvèdre
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Late-ripening and warmth-loving, adding structure, tannin and gamey, leathery notes; about 2,700 ha in 2025
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Cinsault
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Floral and light-bodied, used for rosé and blends; about 2,000 ha
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Carignan
slides.3.highlights.2.content: High acidity and tannin, worthwhile mainly from old vines; about 3,600 ha (more than Mourvèdre)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Counoise and others
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Counoise, Vaccarèse and Muscardin are minor supporting varieties in Châteauneuf-du-Pape
slides.3.content: Areas are 2025 Inter Rhône figures for scale only; quizzes avoid exact hectares.
slides.4.title: The GSM blend
slides.4.highlights.0.title: G: Grenache
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Provides the fruit, roundness and alcohol
slides.4.highlights.1.title: S: Syrah
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Adds colour, tannin, pepper and dark fruit
slides.4.highlights.2.title: M: Mourvèdre
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Adds structure, backbone and ageing potential
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Why blend
slides.4.highlights.3.content: The three complement one another: the point is the division of roles that fixes each other's weaknesses, not a fixed ratio
slides.4.content: GSM is a conceptual shorthand; legal varieties and ratios differ by AOC and come in Level 2.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
Which is the most planted red grape in the Rhône Valley?
Grenache far outweighs Syrah (about 32,000 vs 22,000 ha, 2025).
Which flavour set best fits northern Rhône Syrah?
A. Black pepper, black fruit, violet, olive
Pepper, dark fruit, violet and olive are classic Syrah clues.
In a GSM blend, what is Mourvèdre's main role?
A. Providing structure, tannin and ageing potential
D. Being used only for sparkling
Mourvèdre ripens late with firm tannin, adding backbone to blends.
